w: Prussian kings and German emperors ruled from here for nearly five centuries, until Allied bombs and East German dynamite reduced it to rubble in 1950. The GDR's Palace of the Republic rose here instead, then came down too. What stands now is a 2013 rebuild wearing a modernist face over the Humboldt Forum inside.
_facts: Main residence of Electors of Brandenburg, Kings of Prussia and German Emperors, 1443-1918
Baroque expansion 1689-1713 under Frederick I, architect Andreas Schlüter, 60m dome added 1845
Damaged in Allied WWII bombing, razed by East German authorities in 1950
GDR built the Palace of the Republic on the site; it was demolished in 2009
Exterior reconstructed from 2013 to house the Humboldt Forum, with a modernist east facade

w: Germany's largest Protestant church doubles as a Hohenzollern mausoleum - the crypt below covers almost the entire basement, packed with royal tombs. Built in 1905 for Kaiser Wilhelm II, it survived a WWII bombing raid and a 1975 East German demolition of one wing before the interior was restored by 2002.
s: Germany's biggest church, and a royal crypt too
_facts: Largest Protestant church in Germany, one of Europe's most important dynastic tombs (House of Hohenzollern)
Present building 1894-1905, ordered by Wilhelm II, architect Julius Raschdorff, Renaissance/Baroque Revival
Hohenzollern crypt covers almost the entire basement
Memorial Church section demolished by East German authorities in 1975
Damaged in WWII bombing; interior restored by 2002

w: Home to the Pergamon Altar, this Stripped Classicism landmark on Museum Island earned UNESCO status in 1999 for its very role in shaping what a museum could be. In October 2023 the whole building shut its doors for a renovation expected to run until 2037 at the earliest - the north wing is due back first, in 2027.
s: Home of the Pergamon Altar, closed until the 2030s
_facts: Built 1910-1930 for Wilhelm II, architects Alfred Messel and Ludwig Hoffmann, Stripped Classicism
Part of Museum Island UNESCO World Heritage listing (1999)
Housed the Antikensammlung (Pergamon Altar), Vorderasiatisches Museum, Museum für Islamische Kunst
Closed to visitors entirely from October 2023 for renovation expected to last 14-20 years (to 2037-2043)
North wing expected to reopen in 2027

w: Named for a Tsar who never asked for the honour - Russia's Alexander I, feted after an 1805 visit - this transport hub is reputedly Berlin's single most-visited spot, ahead of even Friedrichstrasse. The TV tower looms over one edge, with the Nikolai Quarter and the Rotes Rathaus just beyond, and the crowds barely thin.
s: Named for a Tsar, ruled by shopping malls
_facts: Named after Russian Tsar Alexander I
Reputedly Berlin's most-visited area, ahead of Friedrichstrasse and City West
Fernsehturm (TV tower), Nikolai Quarter and Rotes Rathaus all nearby
Major commercial area of shopping malls and department stores
Large public square and transport hub in central Mitte

w: Raised to mark one Prussian win over Denmark, then rededicated twice more as Bismarck kept winning them, the column's gilded goddess Victoria - 8.3 metres of bronze - gave Berliners their favourite nickname: Goldelse, 'Golden Lizzy', lifted from an 1866 novel. Climb the 67-metre column and the view opens over the city.
_facts: Designed by Heinrich Strack from 1864 to mark the Prussian victory over Denmark, inaugurated 1873
Later rededicated for victories over Austria (1866) and France (1870-71)
8.3m bronze Victoria statue by Friedrich Drake; total height 67m
Nicknamed 'Goldelse' (Golden Lizzy) after the heroine of an 1866 novel
Ticketed viewing platform overlooks Berlin

w: Once the busiest traffic intersection in Europe, this square was flattened by WWII bombs, then left a literal no-man's-land when the Berlin Wall cut through it. Named for the road to Potsdam that once passed the old city gate here, it sat desolate for decades before glass towers began filling the scar in the 1990s.
_facts: Named after the city of Potsdam, marking where the old road passed through Berlin's city wall
Became one of the busiest traffic intersections in Europe by the early 20th century
Totally destroyed in WWII, then left desolate when the Berlin Wall bisected it
Extensively redeveloped through the 1990s and early 2000s after reunification
Now a commercial/cultural hub of offices, retail, cinemas and hotels

w: Bombed in 1943, the old church's spire was left standing on purpose - Berliners nicknamed the jagged ruin 'der hohle Zahn', the hollow tooth, and it still juts over the Kurfürstendamm beside its boxy 1959-63 replacement. Inside the ruin, a memorial hall keeps the wreckage as the point.
s: The bombed spire Berlin kept on purpose
_facts: Original church built in the 1890s, badly damaged in a 1943 bombing raid
New building constructed 1959-1963 alongside the retained damaged spire
Damaged spire's ground floor made into a memorial hall (Gedächtnishalle)
Located on the Kurfürstendamm at Breitscheidplatz, in the Bikini-Berlin complex
Nicknamed 'der hohle Zahn' (the hollow tooth) by Berliners

w: Berlin's grand ceremonial spine runs dead straight from the old Berlin Palace to the Brandenburg Gate, taking its name from the linden trees still shading the pedestrian median. Nearly every landmark worth seeing in Mitte lines up somewhere along this one boulevard, rivers included.
s: The boulevard that strings Mitte together
_facts: Boulevard in central Mitte, runs from Berlin Palace to Brandenburg Gate
Named after the linden (lime) trees lining the median's pedestrian mall
Links numerous Berlin landmarks and rivers along its length

w: Bombed in the war and left to decay under East German neglect, the Neues Museum's ruined shell was pieced back together by David Chipperfield between 1999 and 2009 - old scars left deliberately visible against the new brickwork. It now holds Berlin's Egyptian and prehistoric collections behind that patched-up history.
s: War scars left visible, on purpose
_facts: Built 1843-1855 for Frederick William IV, architect Friedrich August Stüler, Neoclassical/Renaissance Revival
Damaged in WWII and left to decay under East Germany
Restored 1999-2009 by David Chipperfield
Houses the Egyptian Museum, Papyrus Museum, Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte, and part of the Antikensammlung
Part of the Museum Island UNESCO World Heritage listing (1999)

w: Karl Friedrich Schinkel's 1830 temple to antiquity set the template for what a museum building should look like, its long colonnade facing the old royal palace across the Lustgarten. It now holds Berlin's classical antiquities and part of the coin collection, still doing exactly the job Schinkel designed it for.
_facts: Built 1825-1830 for Frederick William III, architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel, German Neoclassical style
Surrounded by Berlin Cathedral, Berlin Palace and the Zeughaus
Houses the Antikensammlung and part of the Münzkabinett coin collection
Part of the Museum Island UNESCO World Heritage listing (1999)
